newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU Court rejects German, Belgian banana complaints.
newsitem.headline: EU Court rejects German, Belgian banana complaints.

text.p: The European Court of Justice dismissed on Tuesday six separate but related challenges from Germany and Belgium to European Union banana import quotas.

The challenges, combined into two cases, were the latest in a long and unsuccessful series, brought mainly by Germany, to be rejected by the Court since the EU introduced controversial import quotas and licences in 1993.

Germany, Belgium and other critics say the rules favour more expensive producers in the EU and former colonies in Africa, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) countries and work against cheaper Latin American supplies.

In the first case, the Court ruled that the EU's executive European Commission was right to allow extra imports from non-ACP countries after plantations in the French overseas departments of Martinique and Guadeloupe and the Caribbean states of Saint Lucia and Dominica were devastated by Hurricane Debbie.
"It shows there's a margin to compensate for storm damage," a Commission spokesman said, noting that the EU's banana import rules had so far resisted all attacks.

The Court, supported by France, also rejected a second challenge from the Belgian government about what it said were inadequate non-EU banana import quotas for Austria, Finland and Sweden, which only joined the EU in 1995.
Imports of cheaper, so-called "dollar" bananas were increased by 353,000 tonnes to cater for the three new members.
The Court ruled that the quotas were justified.
